facts.fact: On a feature, the Produced By credit belongs to the people primarily responsible for originating and/or managing the picture's production and delivery, making regular, continuous and substantial creative, production, budgetary and legal decisions across the four stages.
In development the producer develops the concept, secures the rights and initial funding, selects the writer and guides development.
In pre-production the producer selects the key creative and physical production team, scouts locations, and oversees the final script, schedule and budget.
In production the producer oversees daily operations, resolves issues raised by the key production and creative staff, and liaises with financiers, studio and distributors.
In post-production and marketing the producer works closely with the post teams and sets marketing and distribution strategy.
The PGA's panel weighs a feature producer's contribution by stage: development 35%, pre-production 20%, production 20%, post-production 25%.
Producing work may be done remotely; physical presence on set is not required for the Producers Mark.

On a television series the producer may conceive the concept or format, pitch it to networks or distributors, choose the director, principal cast, pilot writer and producing team, and help create the series bible.

In series production the producer approves storylines and scripts, approves the hiring of department heads and episodic directors, approves call sheets and schedules, and supervises the amortization and pattern budgets.
In series post-production the producer handles delivery requirements, views dailies and the director's cut, and takes part in approving the final cut of each episode.

On a feature the Line Producer/Co-Producer is the single person with primary responsibility for the budget and logistics from pre-production through production, and all below-the-line department heads report to them.
The Production Manager category includes the DGA-covered Unit Production Manager, who runs day-to-day physical production.

A non-primary feature Executive Producer must have secured an essential portion of the financing (no less than 25%) and/or made a significant contribution to the literary property; someone who only provides or arranges money does not qualify.

The PGA recognises producing work in these formats: feature film, animated feature, documentary feature, short film, scripted episodic TV, non-fiction TV, special event TV, digital short form, video game, special venue, transmedia and immersive media.

In scripted television the producing titles run, by who reports to whom: Executive Producer (reports only to the studio or financier-distributor), Co-Executive Producer, Supervising Producer, Producer, Co-Producer, with the Associate Producer as a support role.

A series Executive Producer is the showrunner or co-showrunner, a creative producer who packaged and sold the series, its creator, a hyphenate who performs critical producing functions, or an experienced line producer.
A Supervising Producer must already have had a writer-producer type credit on a series, or a Producer or Produced By credit, or be the producing-director supervising all episodic directors.
A series Line Producer may, by experience and body of work, be credited Co-Producer, Producer, Produced By, Co-Executive Producer or Executive Producer.
A first-time head of post-production on a scripted series may receive the Associate Producer credit.
The Associate Producer credit is granted sparingly and not to someone who mainly works as an assistant.

The PGA counts as the full producing team: executive producers, producers, co-executive producers, supervising producers, senior producers, line producers, co-producers, associate producers, segment, field and story producers, production managers, VFX producers and coordinators, post-production supervisors and managers, and production and post-production coordinators.
O*NET places producers and directors in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation); 57% of respondents said a new hire needs a bachelor's degree.

The PGA's Debra Hill Fellowship goes, typically once a year, to someone completing an accredited graduate producing program at AFI, Chapman, Columbia College Chicago, Columbia, NYU, North Carolina School of the Arts, University of Arizona, UCLA or USC; the grant varies and pays for overhead and options, not tuition.
value: North Carolina School of the Arts

facts.fact: Sundance's Producers Track takes emerging independent producers with a work-in-progress feature into the yearlong Producers Lab and Fellowship; the 2027 feature lab is at Ucross, Wyoming, July 12-17, 2027, and each fellow receives a grant.
Two producers or producing teams with films premiering at Sundance each receive the Sundance Institute | Amazon MGM Studios Producers Award, a $10,000 grant.
Feature entry to the 2027 Sundance Film Festival costs $80 by July 27, $100 by August 28 and $125 by September 21.
A Sundance feature runs 50 minutes or more; a U.S. feature must have at least half its financing from the United States and keep its world premiere status.
American Film Market 2026 badges cost from $345 for one day to $1,395 for the Platinum badge (November 10-14), and more when bought onsite.

Registering at the Marché du Film (Cannes, 11-19 May 2027) requires a current professional activity in the film industry; the registration page lists the standard Marché badge at €459, €529 or €629 by booking window.

The Marché's Producers Network add-on (+€250) is open only to producers with at least one feature in the past four years that had a commercial theatrical release or an exclusive SVOD acquisition; for the USA only a "producer" credit counts, and it is capped at 370 participants.
No union membership is required to work as a producer; the PGA is a professional association and does not read scripts, find financing or make deals.
No minimum pay is set for producers: the PGA has no industry-wide Minimum Basic Agreement, so pay is negotiated in each producer's personal service contract.
The median wage of producers and directors in 2025 was $43.44 an hour, $90,360 a year.
Producers and directors held 181,000 jobs in 2025; growth for 2025-2035 is projected as average (3% to 4%), with 12,100 projected openings.

The DGA minimum for a Unit Production Manager, July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, is $7,197 a week in the studio and $10,076 on location, plus a weekly production fee of $1,560 or $1,857; by the day $1,799 or $2,519.
The PGA asks companies without another health plan for a producer to budget a direct contribution of at least $3.33 an hour per producer.
In New York's production credit, above-the-line salaries count only up to 40% of all other qualified costs.
The Producers Guild of America is a professional trade association, not a union; in 1985 it was barred from becoming a labor union under the NLRA.

PGA membership needs an individual (not company) producing credit on an eligible production released within the last five years (seven for features and AAA games, ten for animated features), or the p.g.a. mark on two or more features, or an Oscar or PGA Awards nomination applied on within two years.
An application needs three unique references (no agent, manager, lawyer or employee), takes 30 to 90 days, and costs a $50 application fee, a $600 initiation fee and $400 a year in dues.
The PGA has over 8,400 members.
Through the Non-Affiliate Agreement negotiated with the AMPTP in 1985 and widened in 1997, producers on qualifying productions can get Motion Picture Industry Pension & Health Plan benefits.

To qualify for MPI health coverage a producer must be credited Executive Producer, Producer, Associate Producer or Post-Production Supervisor, be hired through a Los Angeles-area office of a signatory employer, and be credited 600 hours (ten weeks) within six months; contributions are made at 60 hours a week, and 400 hours keep coverage each later six-month period.
The producer must file a non-affiliate participation form within 60 days of starting each production, or contributions are waived; documentary, commercial, news and sports work does not count.
The Producers Mark (p.g.a.) is a free certification the PGA licenses film by film to producers who did a major portion of the producing in a decision-making capacity; PGA membership is not needed.
Only a producer contractually and onscreen credited "Produced By" or "Producer" can be considered, and there is no limit on how many receive the Mark.
A film that offered any "producer" credit as a crowdfunding perk is refused the Mark, awards eligibility and as a basis for PGA membership.
Certification takes about six to eight weeks (the PGA says to allow eight to ten) and should be sought late in post once the film is substantively complete.

A disputed Mark goes to a panel of at least two arbiters, each with at least two Producer or Produced By credits; the producers together may strike no more than 10% of the arbiter list, and an appeal goes to at least three fresh arbiters.
An appeal statement is advised at no more than 2,500 words, with 25 pages in all; third parties may send up to 20 pages.
A producer who held the Mark on an original film automatically gets at least 25% credit toward the development phase of a sequel, prequel, remake or spin-off.
A recognised producing partnership can both receive the Mark if one partner did at least 50% of the work and the other at least 25%; the petition is due at least six months before submission.
Close calls on the Mark are decided in favour of inclusion.

For PGA television awards a producer needs an eligible title (Executive Producer, Co-Executive Producer, Supervising Producer, Producer, Produced By) on at least half the season's episodes, with no limit on the number eligible.
A departed showrunner stays eligible if they ran the series through its first season, kept the Executive Producer credit and keep consulting.
Best Picture goes to producers credited "producer" or "produced by" only; executive producers, co-producers, associate and line producers get no nomination.
Best Picture nominees are at most three producers who did the major portion of the producing; a PGA-recognised partnership of two counts as one.
A Best Picture producer nominee must have been found awards-eligible by the PGA or won an appeal; the Academy's Producers Branch Executive Committee makes the final call and may add a producer.
Proof of PGA submission is due by September 14, 2026 for films released January to June 2026 and by November 12, 2026 for July to December.
A Best Picture film needs a seven-day qualifying run in one of six U.S. metro areas, an expanded run in nine more markets, and two of the four Representation and Inclusion Standards.
All active and life Academy members nominate up to ten pictures for Best Picture and vote in the final round.

Emmy program awards go to producers credited Executive Producer, Co-Executive Producer, Supervising Producer, Producer or Produced By on at least 50% of the year's episodes who had substantial or final control of creative and financial matters; studio and network executives are excluded, and representatives unless they meet that control test.
An Emmy program entry costs a $225 processing charge plus $100 per entrant; Outstanding Comedy Series has a cap guideline of 11 entrants and needs at least six episodes in the year.

PGA Awards 2027: films released in 2026 enter by October 9, 2026 for a ballot fee stated as $750.00; series and specials enter by September 25, 2026 for $600, and comedy or drama series need at least six episodes over 20 minutes.
The PGA's determination is relied on by the Academy, the Golden Globes and BAFTA for their producing awards.
A Produced By who is also the director, writer, actor or representative gets the Mark only if, leaving out decisions made in that other role, they did a major portion of the producing.

A director-producer must show regular, continuous and substantial production, budget and legal decisions and at least two of: first on the project or securing its source, securing a writer, key cast or financing before greenlight, or reviving a stalled project; securing themselves does not count.

For a writer-producer, story and script work counts as writing, not producing; they need the same Category A plus at least two Category B contributions beyond a writer's, such as securing a director, cast or financing.
For an actor-producer, work on their own character and marketing as an actor does not count; they need Category A plus at least two Category B contributions.
A manager or agent credited as producer needs Category A plus at least three Category B contributions beyond what representing the client involves.
The producing-partnership rule does not apply if either partner also wrote, directed, acted, managed or financed the picture.
Under the WGA, anyone credited as a producer in any capacity or as director is a "production executive" for writing-credit purposes.
A production executive who is a later writer on an original screenplay needs more than 50% of the final script for credit; on a non-original screenplay, more than 33%.

Proposing a production executive for writing credit alongside other writers triggers an automatic WGA credit arbitration; a production executive claiming team credit must tell the Guild in writing when the team writing begins.
A series Co-Executive Producer who also writes on the show must perform significant producing functions in a decision-making capacity.

topics.topic: Time and money of a project

facts.fact: California's Program 4.0 allocates $750 million in credits a year, running July 1, 2025 through fiscal 2029-30.
California requires 75% of the budget spent or 75% of principal photography days in-state, and a minimum budget of $1 million (per episode for series).

Non-independent projects get 35% on up to $120 million of qualified spend (a $42 million cap), relocating series 40%, and independents 35% on up to $20 million, which they may sell or transfer; uplifts add 5% or 10%.
Producers', writers', directors' and actors' wages are not qualified spending under California's credit.
Once California allocates a credit, principal photography must begin within 180 days (240 for budgets of $100 million or more) and the final element must be delivered within 30 months.
In a California budget, contingency may be up to 10% and a completion bond fee up to 2% of qualified spend; E&O insurance is non-qualified.

New York credits 30% of qualified production costs, funded at $700 million a year through 2036; the minimum budget is $1 million downstate and $250,000 elsewhere, and the application must be in before principal photography.

Georgia's credit is 20% of in-state spend with at least $500,000 of qualified expenditure, plus 10% for a Georgia promotion; it can be sold, and projects certified from 2023 must be audited before use.

Under 26 U.S.C. 181 a producer could expense up to $15 million of a qualified film or series ($20 million in low-income or distressed areas) if 75% of compensation is paid for U.S. services; only the first 44 episodes of a series count.
Section 181 does not apply to productions commencing after December 31, 2025; the 2025 amendment (Pub. L. 119-21) added sound recordings but did not move that date.
MPI health contributions on a theatrical film begin eight weeks before principal photography.
The Through Her Lens program takes only films that can be completed on a $120,000 budget.
Women were 28% of producers and 23% of executive producers on the 250 top-grossing U.S. films of 2025, and 26% of producers on the top 100.
In 2025-26 television, women were 41% of producers and 31% of executive producers on broadcast network programs, and 45% of producers on streaming programs.

Tribeca's Through Her Lens program is for women and non-binary writers and directors, who must be at least 21, live in the U.S. or Puerto Rico and not be students; each project needs an attached producer who is not its director.
In Oregon, individuals 18 or older may form a limited liability company.
In California a 14- to 17-year-old can be emancipated by court and then get a work permit, keep earnings and get a credit card; voting still waits until 18.

Readings: the PGA motion-picture awards rule writes the ballot fee as "seven hundred dollars ($750.00)"; the fact gives the figure as stated, $750.00, and the words disagree. The PGA job-description text and stage weights come from the Producers Mark rules, which share them with the Awards rules. The TV credit ladder is the order of the reporting lines in the PGA Code of Credits, not a stated rank. The O*NET wage and employment figures are for producers and directors together; O*NET gives no percentiles on the summary page. The CA "uplifts add 5% or 10%" covers VFX (5%), out-of-zone (5%) and local-hire labor (10%) as the guidelines list them. No figure here was computed from others.

Not found, with what was tried: BLS OOH "Producers and Directors" and the OEWS 27-2012 table (www.bls.gov answered 403 to the declared client; the BLS public API refused for the shared daily threshold; web.archive.org snapshots 20261021084043 and 20250329222525 exist but every fetch was reset, five tries each) so the percentile distribution (10th to 90th) is not here. The Academy's own oscars.org page (Akamai 403). Georgia's own film office page (georgia.org behind Cloudflare "Just a moment"; not passed). California Family Code 6500, 6700-6751 on minors' contracts and court approval (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov behind Cloudflare; lacourt.org's FAM 172 behind Cloudflare; archive snapshots of the Family Code chapters exist, 20250922213344 and 20250922213331, but fetches reset): so the age of majority, a minor's power to disaffirm, and court approval of a producer's contract are not stated here; only Oregon's LLC age and California's emancipation page are. No primary found on a minor's capacity to take out insurance or a loan. Completion bonds and E&O: no bond company's or distributor's own terms read (Discovery's production guide is behind a login; PBS's handbook pages read hold no insurance limits); only California's budget treatment is here. No producer-specific Academy, Emmy or PGA rule ties eligibility to sex or age (none found in the rules read). Producer representation (agents and managers, their licensing and commission caps), WGA MBA hyphenate terms beyond the Screen Credits Manual, Film Independent's labs and grants (not reached in this turn's budget), Women In Film's Finishing Fund (403), and any measured time to move up the producing ladder were not reached or not found. No strike is in force for producers: the PGA is not a union.
